sentences.heading: Market failure
sentences.text: In neoclassical economics, market failure is a situation in which the allocation of goods and services by a free market is not Pareto efficient, often leading to a net loss of economic value.

sentences.heading: Market failure
sentences.text: The first known use of the term by economists was in 1958, but the concept has been traced back to the Victorian writers John Stuart Mill and Henry Sidgwick.

sentences.heading: Market failure
sentences.text: Market failures are often associated with public goods, time-inconsistent preferences, information asymmetries, failures of competition, principal–agent problems, externalities, unequal bargaining power, behavioral irrationality (in behavioral economics), and macro-economic failures (such as unemployment and inflation).

sentences.heading: Market failure
sentences.text: The neoclassical school attributes market failures to the interference of self-regulatory organizations, governments or supra-national institutions in a particular market, although this view is criticized by heterodox economists.

sentences.heading: Market failure
sentences.text: Economists, especially microeconomists, are often concerned with the causes of market failure and possible means of correction.

sentences.heading: Market failure
sentences.text: Such analysis plays an important role in many types of public policy decisions and studies.

sentences.heading: Market failure
sentences.text: However, government policy interventions, such as taxes, subsidies, wage and price controls, and regulations, may also lead to an inefficient allocation of resources, sometimes called government failure.

sentences.heading: Market failure
sentences.text: Most mainstream economists believe that there are circumstances (like building codes, fire safety regulations or endangered species laws) in which it is possible for government or other organizations to improve the inefficient market outcome.

sentences.heading: Market failure
sentences.text: Several heterodox schools of thought disagree with this as a matter of ideology.

sentences.heading: Market failure
sentences.text: An ecological market failure exists when human activity in a market economy is exhausting critical non-renewable resources, disrupting fragile ecosystems, or overloading biospheric waste absorption capacities.

sentences.heading: Market failure
sentences.text: In none of these cases does the criterion of Pareto efficiency obtain.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories
sentences.text: Different economists have different views about what events are the sources of market failure.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories
sentences.text: Mainstream economic analysis widely accepts that there are several causes of market failures.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories
sentences.text: These include if the market is "monopolised" or a small group of businesses hold significant market power resulting in a "failure of competition"; if production of the good or service results in an externality (external costs or benefits); if the good or service is a "public good"; if there is a "failure of information" or information asymmetry; if there is unequal bargaining power; if there is bounded rationality or irrationality; and if there are macro-economic failures such as unemployment or inflation.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories > Failure of competition
sentences.text: Agents in a market can gain market power, allowing them to block other mutually beneficial gains from trade from occurring.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories > Failure of competition

sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories > Public goods

sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories > Externalities > Coase theorem
sentences.text: The Coase theorem, developed by Ronald Coase and labeled as such by George Stigler, states that private transactions are efficient as long as property rights exist, only a small number of parties are involved, and transactions costs are low.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories > Externalities > Coase theorem
sentences.text: Additionally, this efficiency will take place regardless of who owns the property rights.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories > Externalities > Coase theorem
sentences.text: This theory comes from a section of Coase's Nobel prize-winning work The Problem of Social Cost.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories > Externalities > Coase theorem
sentences.text: While the assumptions of low transactions costs and a small number of parties involved may not always be applicable in real-world markets, Coase's work changed the long-held belief that the owner of property rights was a major determining factor in whether or not a market would fail.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories > Externalities > Coase theorem
sentences.text: The Coase theorem points out when one would expect the market to function properly even when there are externalities.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories > Externalities > Coase theorem
sentences.text: A market is an institution in which individuals or firms exchange not just commodities, but the rights to use them in particular ways for particular amounts of time. sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories > Externalities > Coase theorem
sentences.text: As a result, agents' control over the uses of their goods and services can be imperfect, because the system of rights which defines that control is incomplete.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories > Externalities > Coase theorem
sentences.text: Typically, this falls into two generalized rights – excludability and transferability.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories > Externalities > Coase theorem
sentences.text: Excludability deals with the ability of agents to control who uses their commodity, and for how long – and the related costs associated with doing so.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Categories > Externalities > Coase theorem

sentences.heading: Market failure > Interpretations and policy examples
sentences.text: This form of analysis has also been adopted by the Keynesian or new Keynesian schools in modern macroeconomics, applying it to Walrasian models of general equilibrium in order to deal with failures to attain full employment, or the non-adjustment of prices and wages.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Interpretations and policy examples
sentences.text: Policies to prevent market failure are already commonly implemented in the economy.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Interpretations and policy examples
sentences.text: For example, to prevent information asymmetry, members of the New York Stock Exchange agree to abide by its rules in order to promote a fair and orderly market in the trading of listed securities.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Interpretations and policy examples

sentences.heading: Market failure > Interpretations and policy examples

sentences.heading: Market failure > Interpretations and policy examples

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Public choice
sentences.text: Economists such as Milton Friedman from the Chicago school and others from the Public Choice school, argue that market failure does not necessarily imply that the government should attempt to solve market failures, because the costs of government failure might be worse than those of the market failure it attempts to fix.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Public choice
sentences.text: This failure of government is seen as the result of the inherent problems of democracy and other forms of government perceived by this school and also of the power of special-interest groups (rent seekers) both in the private sector and in the government bureaucracy.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Public choice
sentences.text: Conditions that many would regard as negative are often seen as an effect of subversion of the free market by coercive government intervention.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Public choice
sentences.text: Beyond philosophical objections, a further issue is the practical difficulty that any single decision maker may face in trying to understand (and perhaps predict) the numerous interactions that occur between producers and consumers in any market.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Austrian
sentences.text: Some advocates of laissez-faire capitalism, including many economists of the Austrian School, argue that there is no such phenomenon as "market failure".

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Austrian
sentences.text: Israel Kirzner states that, "Efficiency for a social system means the efficiency with which it permits its individual members to achieve their individual goals."

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Austrian
sentences.text: Inefficiency only arises when means are chosen by individuals that are inconsistent with their desired goals.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Austrian
sentences.text: This definition of efficiency differs from that of Pareto efficiency, and forms the basis of the theoretical argument against the existence of market failures.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Austrian
sentences.text: However, providing that the conditions of the first welfare theorem are met, these two definitions agree, and give identical results.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Austrian
sentences.text: Austrians argue that the market tends to eliminate its inefficiencies through the process of entrepreneurship driven by the profit motive; something the government has great difficulty detecting, or correcting.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Marxian
sentences.text: Objections also exist on more fundamental bases, such as Marxian analysis.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Marxian
sentences.text: Colloquial uses of the term "market failure" reflect the notion of a market "failing" to provide some desired attribute different from efficiency – for instance, high levels of inequality can be considered a "market failure", yet are not Pareto inefficient, and so would not be considered a market failure by mainstream economics.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Marxian
sentences.text: In addition, many Marxian economists would argue that the system of private property rights is a fundamental problem in itself, and that resources should be allocated in another way entirely.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Marxian
sentences.text: This is different from concepts of "market failure" which focuses on specific situations – typically seen as "abnormal" – where markets have inefficient outcomes.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Marxian
sentences.text: Marxists, in contrast, would say that markets have inefficient and democratically unwanted outcomes – viewing market failure as an inherent feature of any capitalist economy – and typically omit it from discussion, preferring to ration finite goods not exclusively through a price mechanism, but based upon need as determined by society expressed through the community.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: In ecological economics, the concept of externalities is considered a misnomer, since market agents are viewed as making their incomes and profits by systematically 'shifting' the social and ecological costs of their activities onto other agents, including future generations.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: Hence, externalities is a modus operandi of the market, not a failure: The market cannot exist without constantly 'failing'.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: The fair and even allocation of non-renewable resources over time is a market failure issue of concern to ecological economics.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: This issue is also known as 'intergenerational fairness'.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: It is argued that the market mechanism fails when it comes to allocating the Earth's finite mineral stock fairly and evenly among present and future generations, as future generations are not, and cannot be, present on today's market.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: In effect, today's market prices do not, and cannot, reflect the preferences of the yet unborn.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: This is an instance of a market failure passed unrecognized by most mainstream economists, as the concept of Pareto efficiency is entirely static (timeless).

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: Imposing government restrictions on the general level of activity in the economy may be the only way of bringing about a more fair and even intergenerational allocation of the mineral stock.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: Hence, Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen and Herman Daly, the two leading theorists in the field, have both called for the imposition of such restrictions: Georgescu-Roegen has proposed a minimal bioeconomic program, and Daly has proposed a comprehensive steady-state economy.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: However, Georgescu-Roegen, Daly, and other economists in the field agree that on a finite Earth, geologic limits will inevitably strain most fairness in the longer run, regardless of any present government restrictions: Any rate of extraction and use of the finite stock of non-renewable mineral resources will diminish the remaining stock left over for future generations to use.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: Another ecological market failure is presented by the overutilisation of an otherwise renewable resource at a point in time, or within a short period of time.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: Such overutilisation usually occurs when the resource in question has poorly defined (or non-existing) property rights attached to it while too many market agents engage in activity simultaneously for the resource to be able to sustain it all.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: Examples range from over-fishing of fisheries and over-grazing of pastures to over-crowding of recreational areas in congested cities.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: This type of ecological market failure is generally known as the 'tragedy of the commons'.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: In this type of market failure, the principle of Pareto efficiency is violated the utmost, as all agents in the market are left worse off, while nobody are benefitting.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: It has been argued that the best way to remedy a 'tragedy of the commons'-type of ecological market failure is to establish enforceable property rights politically – only, this may be easier said than done.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: The issue of climate change presents an overwhelming example of a 'tragedy of the commons'-type of ecological market failure: The Earth's atmosphere may be regarded as a 'global common' exhibiting poorly defined (non-existing) property rights, and the waste absorption capacity of the atmosphere with regard to carbon dioxide is presently being heavily overloaded by a large volume of emissions from the world economy.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: Historically, the fossil fuel dependence of the Industrial Revolution has unintentionally thrown mankind out of ecological equilibrium with the rest of the Earth's biosphere (including the atmosphere), and the market has failed to correct the situation ever since.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: Quite the opposite: The unrestricted market has been exacerbating this global state of ecological dis-equilibrium, and is expected to continue doing so well into the foreseeable future.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: This particular market failure may be remedied to some extent at the political level by the establishment of an international (or regional) cap and trade property rights system, where carbon dioxide emission permits are bought and sold among market agents.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Ecological
sentences.text: The term 'uneconomic growth' describes a pervasive ecological market failure: The ecological costs of further economic growth in a so-called 'full-world economy' like the present world economy may exceed the immediate social benefits derived from this growth.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Zerbe and McCurdy
sentences.text: "A fundamental problem with the concept of market failure, as economists occasionally recognize, is that it describes a situation that exists everywhere."

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Zerbe and McCurdy
sentences.text: Transaction costs are part of each market exchange, although the price of transaction costs is not usually determined.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Zerbe and McCurdy
sentences.text: They occur everywhere and are unpriced.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Zerbe and McCurdy
sentences.text: Consequently, market failures and externalities can arise in the economy every time transaction costs arise.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Zerbe and McCurdy
sentences.text: There is no place for government intervention.

sentences.heading: Market failure > Objections > Zerbe and McCurdy
sentences.text: Instead, government should focus on the elimination of both transaction costs and costs of provision.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: In economics, an externality is a cost or benefit to an uninvolved third party that arises as an effect of another party's (or parties') activity.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: Many externalities can be considered as unpriced components that are involved in either consumer or producer consumption.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: Air pollution from motor vehicles is one example.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: The cost of air pollution to society is not paid by either the producers or users of motorized transport.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: Water pollution from mills and factories are another example.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: All (water) consumers are made worse off by pollution but are not compensated by the market for this damage.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: The concept of externality was first developed by Alfred Marshall in the 1890s and achieved broader attention in the works of economist Arthur Pigou in the 1920s.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: The prototypical example of a negative externality is environmental pollution.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: Pigou argued that a tax, equal to the marginal damage or marginal external cost, (later called a "Pigouvian tax") on negative externalities could be used to reduce their incidence to an efficient level.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: Subsequent thinkers have debated whether it is preferable to tax or to regulate negative externalities, the optimally efficient level of the Pigouvian taxation, and what factors cause or exacerbate negative externalities, such as providing investors in corporations with limited liability for harms committed by the corporation.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: Externalities often occur when the production or consumption of a product or service's private price equilibrium cannot reflect the true costs or benefits of that product or service for society as a whole.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: This causes the externality competitive equilibrium to not adhere to the condition of Pareto optimality.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: Thus, since resources can be better allocated, externalities are an example of market failure.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: Externalities can be either positive or negative.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: Governments and institutions often take actions to internalize externalities, thus market-priced transactions can incorporate all the benefits and costs associated with transactions between economic agents.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: The most common way this is done is by imposing taxes on the producers of the externality.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: However, since regulators do not always have all the information on the externality, it can be difficult to impose the right tax.

sentences.heading: Externality
sentences.text: Once the externality is internalized through a tax, the competitive equilibrium is Pareto optimal.

sentences.heading: Externality > History of the concept
sentences.text: The term "externality" was first coined by the British economist Alfred Marshall in his seminal work, "Principles of Economics," published in 1890.

sentences.heading: Externality > History of the concept
sentences.text: Marshall introduced the concept to elucidate the effects of production and consumption activities that extend beyond the immediate parties involved in a transaction.

sentences.heading: Externality > History of the concept
sentences.text: Marshall's formulation of externalities laid the groundwork for subsequent scholarly inquiry into the broader societal impacts of economic actions.

sentences.heading: Externality > History of the concept
sentences.text: While Marshall provided the initial conceptual framework for externalities, it was Arthur Pigou, a British economist, who further developed the concept in his influential work, "The Economics of Welfare," published in 1920.

sentences.heading: Externality > History of the concept
sentences.text: Pigou expanded upon Marshall's ideas and introduced the concept of "Pigovian taxes" or corrective taxes aimed at internalizing externalities by aligning private costs with social costs.

sentences.heading: Externality > History of the concept
sentences.text: His work emphasized the role of government intervention in addressing market failures resulting from externalities.

sentences.heading: Externality > History of the concept
sentences.text: Additionally, the American economist Frank Knight contributed to the understanding of externalities through his writings on social costs and benefits in the 1920s and 1930s.

sentences.heading: Externality > History of the concept
sentences.text: Knight's work highlighted the inherent challenges in quantifying and mitigating externalities within market systems, underscoring the complexities involved in achieving optimal resource allocation.

sentences.heading: Externality > History of the concept
sentences.text: Throughout the 20th century, the concept of externalities continued to evolve with advancements in economic theory and empirical research.

sentences.heading: Externality > History of the concept
sentences.text: Scholars such as Ronald Coase and Harold Hotelling made significant contributions to the understanding of externalities and their implications for market efficiency and welfare.

sentences.heading: Externality > History of the concept
sentences.text: The recognition of externalities as a pervasive phenomenon with wide-ranging implications has led to its incorporation into various fields beyond economics, including environmental science, public health, and urban planning.

sentences.heading: Externality > History of the concept
sentences.text: Contemporary debates surrounding issues such as climate change, pollution, and resource depletion underscore the enduring relevance of the concept of externalities in addressing pressing societal challenges.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: A negative externality is any difference between the private cost of an action or decision to an economic agent and the social cost.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: In simple terms, a negative externality is anything that causes an indirect cost to individuals.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: An example is the toxic gases that are released from industries or mines, these gases cause harm to individuals within the surrounding area and have to bear a cost (indirect cost) to get rid of that harm.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: Conversely, a positive externality is any difference between the private benefit of an action or decision to an economic agent and the social benefit.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: A positive externality is anything that causes an indirect benefit to individuals and for which the producer of that positive externality is not compensated.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: For example, planting trees makes individuals' property look nicer and it also cleans the surrounding areas.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: In microeconomic theory, externalities are factored into competitive equilibrium analysis as the social effect, as opposed to the private market which only factors direct economic effects.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: The social effect of economic activity is the sum of the indirect (the externalities) and direct factors.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: The Pareto optimum, therefore, is at the levels in which the social marginal benefit equals the social marginal cost.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: Externalities are the residual effects of economic activity on persons not directly participating in the transaction.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: The consequences of producer or consumer behaviors that result in external costs or advantages imposed on others are not taken into account by market pricing and can have both positive and negative effects.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: To further elaborate on this, when expenses associated with the production or use of an item or service are incurred by others but are not accounted for in the market price, this is known as a negative externality.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: The health and well-being of local populations may be negatively impacted by environmental deterioration resulting from the extraction of natural resources.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: Comparably, the tranquility of surrounding inhabitants might be disturbed by noise pollution from industry or transit, which lowers their quality of life.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: On the other hand, positive externalities occur when the activities of producers or consumers benefit other parties in ways that are not accounted for in market exchanges.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: A prime example of a positive externality is education, as those who invest in it gain knowledge and production for society as a whole in addition to personal profit.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: Government involvement is frequently necessary to address externalities.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: This can be done by enacting laws, Pigovian taxes, or other measures that encourage positive externalities or internalize external costs.

sentences.heading: Externality > Definitions
sentences.text: Through the integration of externalities into economic research and policy formulation, society may endeavor to get results that optimize aggregate well-being and foster sustainable growth.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: A voluntary exchange may reduce societal welfare if external costs exist.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: The person who is affected by the negative externalities in the case of air pollution will see it as lowered utility: either subjective displeasure or potentially explicit costs, such as higher medical expenses.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: The externality may even be seen as a trespass on their health or violating their property rights (by reduced valuation).

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: Thus, an external cost may pose an ethical or political problem.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: Negative externalities are Pareto inefficient, and since Pareto efficiency underpins the justification for private property, they undermine the whole idea of a market economy.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: For these reasons, negative externalities are more problematic than positive externalities.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: Although positive externalities may appear to be beneficial, while Pareto efficient, they still represent a failure in the market as it results in the production of the good falling under what is optimal for the market.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: By allowing producers to recognise and attempt to control their externalities production would increase as they would have motivation to do so.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: With this comes the free rider problem.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: The free rider problem arises when people overuse a shared resource without doing their part to produce or pay for it.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: It represents a failure in the market where goods and services are not able to be distributed efficiently, allowing people to take more than what is fair.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: For example, if a farmer has honeybees a positive externality of owning these bees is that they will also pollinate the surrounding plants.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: This farmer has a next door neighbour who also benefits from this externality even though he does not have any bees himself.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: From the perspective of the neighbour he has no incentive to purchase bees himself as he is already benefiting from them at zero cost.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: But for the farmer, he is missing out on the full benefits of his own bees which he paid for, because they are also being used by his neighbour.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: There are a number of theoretical means of improving overall social utility when negative externalities are involved.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: The market-driven approach to correcting externalities is to internalize third party costs and benefits, for example, by requiring a polluter to repair any damage caused.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: But in many cases, internalizing costs or benefits is not feasible, especially if the true monetary values cannot be determined.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: Laissez-faire economists such as Friedrich Hayek and Milton Friedman sometimes refer to externalities as "neighborhood effects" or "spillovers", although externalities are not necessarily minor or localized.

sentences.heading: Externality > Implications
sentences.text: Similarly, Ludwig von Mises argues that externalities arise from lack of "clear personal property definition."

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Positional
sentences.text: The sociological basis of positional externalities is rooted in the theories of conspicuous consumption and positional goods.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Positional
sentences.text: Conspicuous consumption (originally articulated by Veblen, 1899) refers to the consumption of goods or services primarily for the purpose of displaying social status or wealth.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Positional
sentences.text: In simpler terms, individuals engage in conspicuous consumption to signal their economic standing or to gain social recognition.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Positional
sentences.text: Positional goods (introduced by Hirsch, 1977) are such goods, whose value is heavily contingent upon how they compare to similar goods owned by others.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Positional
sentences.text: Their desirability is or derived utility is intrinsically tied to their relative scarcity or exclusivity within a particular social context.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Positional
sentences.text: The economic concept of Positional externalities originates from Duesenberry's Relative Income Hypothesis.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Positional
sentences.text: This hypothesis challenges the conventional microeconomic model, as outlined by the Common Pool Resource (CPR) mechanism, which typically assumes that an individual's utility derived from consuming a particular good or service remains unaffected by other's consumption choices.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Positional
sentences.text: Instead, Duesenberry posits that individuals gauge the utility of their consumption based on a comparison with other consumption bundles, thus introducing the notion of relative income into economic analysis.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Positional
sentences.text: Consequently, the consumption of positional goods becomes highly sought after, as it directly impacts one's perceived status relative to others in their social circle.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Positional
sentences.text: Example: consider a scenario where individuals within a social group vie for the latest luxury cars.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Positional
sentences.text: As one member acquires a top-of-the-line vehicle, others may feel compelled to upgrade their own cars to preserve their status within the group.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Positional
sentences.text: This cycle of competitive consumption can result in inefficient allocation of resources and exacerbate income inequality within society.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Positional
sentences.text: The consumption of positional goods engenders negative externalities, wherein the acquisition of such goods by one individual diminishes the utility or value of similar goods held by others within the same reference group.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Positional
sentences.text: This positional externality, can lead to a cascade of overconsumption, as individuals strive to maintain or improve their relative position through excessive spending.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Positional
sentences.text: Positional externalities are related, but not similar to Pecuniary externalities.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Pecuniary
sentences.text: Pecuniary externalities are those which affect a third party's profit but not their ability to produce or consume.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Pecuniary
sentences.text: These externalities "occur when new purchases alter the relevant context within which an existing positional good is evaluated."

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Inframarginal
sentences.text: The concept of inframarginal externalities was introduced by James Buchanan and Craig Stubblebine in 1962.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Inframarginal
sentences.text: Inframarginal externalities differ from other externalities in that there is no benefit or loss to the marginal consumer.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Inframarginal

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Inframarginal

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Inframarginal

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Technological

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Technological
sentences.text: These externalities occur when technology spillovers from the acts of one economic agent impact the production or consumption potential of another agency.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Technological
sentences.text: Depending on their nature, these spillovers may produce positive or negative externalities.

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Technological

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Technological

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Technological

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Technological

sentences.heading: Externality > Examples > Technological

sentences.text: When resources are managed poorly or there are no well-defined property rights, externalities frequently result, especially when it comes to common pool resources.

sentences.heading: Externality > Causes
sentences.text: This phenomenon—famously referred to by Garrett Hardin as the "tragedy of the commons"—highlights people's propensity to put their immediate self-interests ahead of the sustainability of shared resources.

sentences.heading: Externality > Causes

sentences.heading: Externality > Causes

sentences.heading: Externality > Causes

sentences.heading: Externality > Causes

sentences.heading: Externality > Causes

sentences.heading: Externality > Causes

sentences.heading: Externality > Causes

sentences.heading: Externality > Causes

sentences.heading: Externality > Causes

sentences.text: Private markets, such as the cell phone industry, offer an efficient way to put buyers and sellers together and determine what goods they produce, how they produce them and who gets them.

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Externalities

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Externalities

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Externalities

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Externalities

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Externalities
sentences.text: The effect of a market exchange on a third party who is outside or “external” to the exchange is called an externality.

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Externalities
sentences.text: Because externalities that occur in market transactions affect other parties beyond those involved, they are sometimes called spillovers.

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Externalities

sentences.text: Let’s say that, if these pollutants were emitted into the air and water, they would create costs of $100 per refrigerator produced.

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Pollution as a Negative Externality
sentences.text: These costs might occur because of adverse effects on human health, property values, or wildlife habitat, reduction of recreation possibilities, or because of other negative impacts.

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Pollution as a Negative Externality
sentences.text: In a market with no anti-pollution restrictions, firms can dispose of certain wastes absolutely free.

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Pollution as a Negative Externality
sentences.text: Now imagine that firms which produce refrigerators must factor in these external costs of pollution—that is, the firms have to consider not only labor and material costs, but also the broader costs to society of harm to health and other costs caused by pollution.

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Work It Out > Identifying the Equilibrium Price and Quantity
sentences.text: If no externalities existed, private costs would be the same as the costs to society as a whole, and private benefits would be the same as the benefits to society as a whole.

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Work It Out > Identifying the Equilibrium Price and Quantity
sentences.text: Thus, if no externalities existed, the interaction of demand and supply will coordinate social costs and benefits.

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Work It Out > Identifying the Equilibrium Price and Quantity
sentences.text: However, when the externality of pollution exists, the supply curve no longer represents all social costs.

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Work It Out > Identifying the Equilibrium Price and Quantity
sentences.text: Because externalities represent a case where markets no longer consider all social costs, but only some of them, economists commonly refer to externalities as an example of market failure.

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Work It Out > Identifying the Equilibrium Price and Quantity
sentences.text: When there is market failure, the private market fails to achieve efficient output, because either firms do not account for all costs incurred in the production of output and/or consumers do not account for all benefits obtained (a positive externality).

sentences.heading: 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > 12.1 The Economics of Pollution > Work It Out > Identifying the Equilibrium Price and Quantity
sentences.text: In the case of pollution, at the market output, social costs of production exceed social benefits to consumers, and the market produces too much of the product.

sections.outcome: Explain what market failure is and why externalities are one cause of it

keyIdeas.statement: Market failure occurs when a free market does not allocate goods and services efficiently.
keyIdeas.explanation: In economic terms, the allocation is not Pareto efficient, so resources could be allocated more effectively.
keyIdeas.example: Externalities are a recognised source of market failure.

evidence.snippet: the allocation of goods and services by a free market is not Pareto efficient
if production of the good or service results in an externality

keyIdeas.statement: An externality is a cost or benefit created by an activity that affects a third party outside the transaction.
keyIdeas.explanation: The affected person or group did not choose to take part in the original exchange, and the effect may be positive or negative.
keyIdeas.example: Air pollution from motor vehicles imposes costs on society that are not paid by the producers or users of transport.

evidence.snippet: a cost or benefit to an uninvolved third party
The cost of air pollution to society is not paid by either the producers or users
Externalities can be either positive or negative.

keyIdeas.statement: Externalities cause market failure when market prices omit costs or benefits that matter to society.
keyIdeas.explanation: The private market outcome then differs from the socially relevant outcome, meaning resources are not allocated in the most efficient way.
keyIdeas.example: Pollution from a factory can make water consumers worse off without compensating them through the market.

evidence.snippet: private price equilibrium cannot reflect the true costs or benefits
since resources can be better allocated, externalities are an example of market failure.
All (water) consumers are made worse off by pollution but are not compensated

misconceptions.correction: Externalities may be negative, such as pollution, or positive, such as the wider gains from vaccines or education.

evidence.snippet: Externalities can be either positive or negative.
Positive externalities tend to be goods like vaccines, schools

misconceptions.belief: Any cost or benefit linked to a product is an externality.
misconceptions.correction: It is an externality only when the effect falls on someone who was not involved in the original market transaction.

evidence.snippet: a cost or benefit to an uninvolved third party
imposed on a third-party that did not take part in the original market transaction

vocabulary.sense: efficiency in the allocation of goods and services
vocabulary.definition: A condition in which the free-market allocation of goods and services meets the relevant efficiency criterion.

evidence.snippet: the allocation of goods and services by a free market is not Pareto efficient

vocabulary.sense: an effect of production or consumption on an uninvolved third party
vocabulary.definition: A cost or benefit from an economic activity that falls on someone outside the market transaction.

evidence.snippet: a cost or benefit to an uninvolved third party that arises as an effect

vocabulary.sense: including external costs or benefits in market decisions
vocabulary.definition: To make the prices paid in transactions reflect all the relevant costs and benefits.

evidence.snippet: market-priced transactions can incorporate all the benefits and costs

questions.stem: What is meant by an externality?
questions.answer: It is a cost or benefit from an economic activity that affects an uninvolved third party.
questions.reasoning: The defining feature is that the effect falls outside the original market transaction.

evidence.snippet: a cost or benefit to an uninvolved third party

questions.stem: Explain why air pollution from motor vehicles can be an externality.
questions.answer: It creates a cost for society, while neither the transport producers nor users pay that cost through the market.
questions.reasoning: The pollution affects people outside the purchase and sale of transport, so it is an external cost.

evidence.snippet: The cost of air pollution to society is not paid by either the producers or users

questions.stem: A vaccination programme creates benefits for people beyond those who receive the vaccinations. How should this externality be classified?
questions.reasoning: Vaccines are given as an example of an activity that tends to create gains for the wider public.

evidence.snippet: Positive externalities tend to be goods like vaccines

questions.stem: Explain why an externality is a cause of market failure rather than merely an effect on a third party.
questions.answer: The market price may leave out the external cost or benefit, so the competitive outcome does not satisfy Pareto optimality and resources could be allocated better.
questions.reasoning: The third-party effect becomes a market failure when the private market outcome fails to account for its wider social consequences.

evidence.snippet: private price equilibrium cannot reflect the true costs or benefits
since resources can be better allocated, externalities are an example of market failure.

sections.outcome: Distinguish private, external and social costs and benefits in negative and positive externalities

keyIdeas.statement: A private cost or benefit is the direct economic effect experienced by the person or firm making a decision.
keyIdeas.explanation: The private market records effects on the participants themselves, rather than consequences for other people.
keyIdeas.example: A firm considers its own production costs, while buyers and sellers consider the direct benefits of their exchange.

evidence.snippet: the private market which only factors direct economic effects

keyIdeas.statement: An external cost or benefit is an indirect effect of an economic activity on people outside the transaction.
keyIdeas.explanation: It is not normally included in the market price, so an unrelated third party may bear a cost or receive a benefit without being paid.
keyIdeas.example: Industrial noise can reduce local residents’ quality of life, even though they are not involved in the industrial transaction.

evidence.snippet: an economic activity that imposes a negative effect on an unrelated third party, not captured by the market price
the tranquility of surrounding inhabitants might be disturbed by noise pollution from industry or transit

keyIdeas.statement: Social cost and benefit combine the direct private effect with the relevant external effect.
keyIdeas.explanation: A negative externality makes social cost greater than private cost; a positive externality makes social benefit greater than private benefit.
keyIdeas.example: Planting trees can create a private benefit for the planter and additional benefits for other people through cleaner surroundings.

evidence.snippet: The social effect of economic activity is the sum of the indirect (the externalities) and direct factors.
planting trees makes individuals' property look nicer and it also cleans the surrounding areas

misconceptions.belief: The market price necessarily includes every cost and benefit created by an activity.
misconceptions.correction: Market pricing can omit effects imposed on other people, so the social effect may differ from the private market effect.

evidence.snippet: the private market which only factors direct economic effects
expenses associated with the production or use of an item or service are incurred by others but are not accounted for in the market price

misconceptions.belief: Externalities occur only when firms produce goods.
misconceptions.correction: Externalities may arise from production or consumption, and may be harmful or beneficial.

evidence.snippet: It can arise either during the production or the consumption of a good or service.
Externalities can be negative or positive.

vocabulary.sense: The direct cost or benefit experienced by the decision-maker in an economic activity.
vocabulary.definition: The effect considered by the individual or firm taking part in the decision, without adding effects on outsiders.

evidence.snippet: the private market which only factors direct economic effects

vocabulary.sense: The total cost or benefit to society, including direct and indirect effects.
vocabulary.definition: The private effect plus any effect imposed on, or received by, other people.

evidence.snippet: The social effect of economic activity is the sum of the indirect (the externalities) and direct factors.

vocabulary.sense: An indirect cost or benefit affecting a third party outside the transaction.
vocabulary.definition: A consequence of production or consumption for someone not directly involved, which the market price does not include.

evidence.snippet: The effect of a market exchange on a third party who is outside or “external” to the exchange is called an externality.

questions.stem: What is meant by a private cost or benefit?
questions.answer: It is the direct economic effect experienced by the person or firm making the decision.
questions.reasoning: Private-market analysis records direct effects on the participants rather than indirect effects on outsiders.

evidence.snippet: the private market which only factors direct economic effects

questions.stem: Explain why pollution affecting local residents is a negative externality rather than a private cost.
questions.answer: It harms people outside the transaction, and that indirect cost is not included in the market price.
questions.reasoning: A negative externality is an external cost imposed on an unrelated third party; a private cost is borne directly by the decision-maker.

evidence.snippet: it imposes costs on people who are "external" to the producer and consumer of the polluting product.

questions.stem: A firm’s activity gives local residents an unpriced benefit. Is this a negative or positive externality? Explain your answer.
questions.answer: It is a positive externality because people outside the transaction benefit without the effect being accounted for in the market exchange.
questions.reasoning: Positive externalities benefit other parties, whereas negative externalities impose costs on them.

evidence.snippet: positive externalities occur when the activities of producers or consumers benefit other parties in ways that are not accounted for in market exchanges

questions.stem: Why can the socially efficient outcome differ from the outcome suggested by private costs and benefits?
questions.answer: Private analysis includes direct effects only, whereas social analysis also includes external costs and benefits; the social effect is therefore the combined effect.
questions.reasoning: Externalities are consequences for third parties that market pricing may omit. The socially efficient level is identified where social marginal benefit equals social marginal cost.

evidence.snippet: the Pareto optimum, therefore, is at the levels in which the social marginal benefit equals the social marginal cost.

sections.outcome: Explain, using a diagram, how a negative externality causes overproduction and a welfare loss

keyIdeas.statement: A production-side negative externality is shown with two supply curves: marginal private cost and marginal social cost.
keyIdeas.explanation: The social-cost curve includes the firm's own production costs plus the pollution costs imposed on society, so it lies above the private-cost curve by the external cost.
keyIdeas.example: In steel production, air and water pollution create the gap between the two supply curves.

evidence.snippet: Whenever an externality arises on the production side, there will be two supply curves (private and social cost).
The social costs include the private costs of production that a company incurs and the external costs of pollution that pass on to society.

keyIdeas.statement: The unregulated market produces at Qp, whereas the socially efficient outcome is Qs, where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost.
keyIdeas.explanation: Consumers and firms base their decisions on private costs, so the market equilibrium does not include the pollution cost. The efficient output includes that wider social cost.
keyIdeas.example: For steel, the market outcome is labelled Pp and Qp, while the efficient outcome is labelled Ps and Qs.

evidence.snippet: They will end up at price Pp and quantity Qp, instead of the more efficient price Ps and quantity Qs.
production should be increased only as long as the marginal social benefit exceeds the marginal social cost

keyIdeas.statement: Because Qp is greater than Qs, the market overproduces and creates a welfare loss.
keyIdeas.explanation: At quantities between Qs and Qp, the social cost is greater than the social benefit. Those units reduce society's welfare because they should not have been produced.
keyIdeas.example: The steel output between Qp and Qs represents production that would leave society better off if it were avoided.

evidence.snippet: at the quantity Qp, the social benefit is less than the social cost
society as a whole would be better off if the goods between Qp and Qs had not been produced.

misconceptions.belief: A negative production externality is represented by adding a second demand curve.
misconceptions.correction: For a production-side externality, the additional curve is a social-cost supply curve; two demand curves are used when the externality comes from consumption.

evidence.snippet: Whenever an externality arises on the production side, there will be two supply curves (private and social cost).

misconceptions.belief: The competitive market automatically reaches the socially efficient output when pollution is free to firms.
misconceptions.correction: If firms and consumers consider only private costs, the market reaches Qp rather than Qs, and social benefit is below social cost at Qp.

evidence.snippet: If the consumers only take into account their own private cost, they will end up at price Pp and quantity Qp
pollution is not something solved by competitive markets.

workedExamples.problem: Refrigerator firms can pollute at no charge. The market initially sells each refrigerator for $650 and produces 45,000. Pollution costs society $100 per refrigerator. Find the new socially priced outcome when firms must pay this external cost.
steps: Add the pollution cost of $100 to the firm's private production cost for every refrigerator.
Show this by shifting the whole private supply curve upwards by $100 to obtain the social supply curve.
Read the new equilibrium from the diagram: the price becomes $700 per refrigerator and output falls to 40,000 refrigerators.
Compare the two outputs: the original market produced 5,000 more refrigerators than the new outcome, so the unregulated market overproduced relative to the social outcome.

questions.stem: What type of externality is pollution from production?
questions.reasoning: Pollution is identified as a negative externality because it creates costs for society.

evidence.snippet: Pollution is a negative externality.

questions.stem: Explain why a production-side negative externality is shown by two supply curves rather than two demand curves.
questions.answer: Production creates two relevant costs: marginal private cost and marginal social cost. Two demand curves are used for a consumption-side externality.
questions.reasoning: The additional curve depends on where the externality arises. Pollution from production creates a gap between private and social cost.

evidence.snippet: if the externality arises on the consumption side, there will be two demand curves instead
The marginal private cost is less than the marginal social or public cost by the amount of the external cost

questions.stem: A factory's private-cost equilibrium is Qp, while its socially efficient equilibrium is Qs. Which output is associated with overproduction, and why?
questions.answer: Qp is the overproduction outcome because Qp is greater than Qs and, at Qp, social cost exceeds social benefit.
questions.reasoning: The market considers private costs, whereas the efficient outcome requires marginal social benefit to equal marginal social cost.

evidence.snippet: at the quantity Qp, the social benefit is less than the social cost
the marginal social benefit should equal the marginal social cost

questions.stem: Using a diagram, judge whether the output between Qs and Qp should be produced in a free market with a negative production externality.
questions.answer: It should not be produced. In this range, social cost is greater than social benefit, so avoiding these units would leave society better off; this is the welfare loss from overproduction.
questions.reasoning: The market output extends beyond the efficient quantity. The lost welfare is the benefit society could have retained by avoiding units from Qs to Qp.

evidence.snippet: society as a whole would be better off if the goods between Qp and Qs had not been produced.
people are buying and consuming too much steel.
